name: Less-Is-Better Effect
description: An option can look better when judged on its own than it does when compared side by side with an objectively superior alternative. Separate evaluation can reverse what feels better because people lean on different cues when direct comparison is absent.
design_relevance_note: Useful for bundle design, comparison cards, single-offer landing pages, review summaries, and marketplace listings: users can overvalue a smaller or objectively worse option when they see it alone, then reverse once a direct comparison is available.
prevalence_note: Known in behavioral-economics and consumer-judgment circles and occasionally very useful for comparison-interface design, but rarely named in everyday mainstream UX critique.

findings.description: A preregistered close replication of Hsee (1998) found support across all replicated studies for the less-is-better effect in separate evaluation: people sometimes rated the objectively smaller/lesser option more highly when judging it alone, even though joint comparison restored a clearer preference for the objectively better option.
findings.effect_size: N = 403; replication d = 0.99, 0.32, and 0.76 across the replicated less-is-better studies
findings.source_title: "Less Is Better" in Separate Evaluations Versus "More Is Better" in Joint Evaluations: Mostly Successful Close Replication and Extension of Hsee (1998)
